{{Short description|Mathematical drawing instrument}}

[[File:Marquois_Scales.jpg|thumb|Marquois scales in a case of drawing instruments (top) and on their own (bottom)]]

'''Marquois scales''' (also known as '''Marquois parallel scales''' or '''Marquois scale and triangle''' or '''military scales''') are a mathematical instrument that found widespread use in Britain, particularly in military [[surveying]], from the late 18th century to [[World War II]].<ref>{{cite book |last1=Gaynor |first1=James M. |title=Mr. Marquois's Most Useful Pair of Scales |date=2015 |publisher=The Tools and Trades Historical Society |isbn=978-0-947673-24-6 |page=9}}</ref>

==Description==
Invented around 1778 by [[Thomas Marquois]], the Marquois scales consist of a right-angle triangle (with sides at a 3:1 ratio) and two rulers (each with multiple [[scale ruler|scales]]).<ref name="elementary geometry" >{{cite book |last1=Winter |first1=Samuel H. |title=Elementary Geometrical Drawing. Part I. Containing Practical Plane Geometry, The Construction and Use of Scales, The Sector, The Protractor, And the Marquois Scales. |date=1887 |publisher=Longmans, Green, and Co. |location=London |pages=107–108 |edition=13th |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=kXULAAAAYAAJ}}</ref> The system could be used to aid precision when marking distances off scales, and to rapidly draw parallel lines a precise distance apart.<ref name="Stanley 1878" >{{cite book |last1=Stanley |first1=William Ford |title=A Descriptive Treatise on Mathematical Drawing Instruments |date=1878 |publisher=E. & F. N. Spon |location=New York |pages=210–214 |edition=Fifth |url=http://www.compleatsurveyor.com/resources/eReference-Library/Surveying-Instrument-Catalogues/Stanley-1878.pdf}}</ref> Quick construction of precise parallel lines was useful in cartography and engineering (especially before the availability of [[graph paper]]) and Marquois scales were convenient in some challenging environments where larger equipment like a [[drawing board]] and [[T-square]] was impractical, such as field survey work and classrooms.<ref name="gazette-1905" /> Marquois scales fell out of favour among draftsmen in the early 20th century,<ref>{{cite book | last1=Bogle | first1=J. du T. | author2=Osbert Chadwick | author3=Reginald Empson Middleton | date=1911 | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=TiNMAAAAMAAJ&dq=%22Marquois+Scales%22&pg=PA2 | title=A Treatise on Surveying | volume=2 | page=2 | publisher=E. & F. N. Spon}}</ref> although familiarity with their use was an entry requirement for the [[Royal Military Academy, Woolwich|Royal Military Academy]] at Woolwich around the same time.<ref name="gazette-1905">{{cite journal |title=Commissions for London University Candidates. Special Requirements for Candidates for the Royal Artillery. |journal=The Mathematical Gazette |date=May 1905 |volume=3 |issue=51 |pages=190–192 |doi=10.1017/S0025557200242198 |jstor=3603903 |s2cid=250433177 |url=http://www.jstor.org/stable/3603903|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Material==
Marquois scales were normally made of [[boxwood]], though sets were sometimes made in [[ivory]]<ref>{{cite web |title=Marquois Scales |url=https://www.mhs.ox.ac.uk/sis25/objects.php?id=16 |website=Scientific Instrument Society 25th Anniversary Exhibition |publisher=History of Science Museum |access-date=26 December 2021}}</ref> or metal.

==Use==
The triangle would be used for many regular [[set square]] operations, the rulers likewise would function as rulers, but the unique function was the 3:1 reduction ratio between measured distance and drawn line.<ref name="elementary geometry" /><ref name="Stanley 1878" />{{rp|210–214}}

A line is drawn along the beveled edge (the side of middle-length) of the triangle. By placing a ruler against the [[hypotenuse]] of the triangle and sliding the triangle along the ruler for 3 units of the ruler's scale, drawing another line along the beveled edge results in a parallel line with a distance of only 1 unit from the original line.<ref name="elementary geometry" /> Using larger distances on a ruler to draw lines smaller distances apart means that margin of error reading off the scale is reduced. Additionally, the end-state is the instruments already in place to slide the triangle again to quickly draw additional lines as desired. A similar method also allows the distance between points on plans or maps to be measured with increased precision.<ref name="elementary geometry" /><ref name="Stanley 1878" />{{rp|210–214}}

Regular set square triangles differ (from a Marquois scales triangle) by being made and used according to the angles of their triangle (e.g. 45-45-90 or 30-60-90 degrees) rather than according to the ratio between the lengths of their sides. Likewise the scales on other rulers are usually intended to be used directly and the selection differs accordingly.<ref name="elementary geometry" /><ref name="Stanley 1878" />{{rp|182, 210–214}}
